reasons: Numerics verified (gradient mean over 8 shards equals big-batch gradient to 8e-17; sum is 8x; ragged-chunk error 1.8e-3 vs gradient magnitude 4.6e-2; sqrt rule 0.283).
The sub-question 'when gradient accumulation is the better option' is not actually answered: the text only says accumulation keeps BN at 256 and is the closest stand-in.
Warmup length 'roughly 500 to 2000 steps' is not consistent with '3 to 5 epochs' for any stated dataset size (ImageNet-1k at batch 2048 is about 625 steps/epoch, i.e. 1,900-3,100 steps).

issues.claim: Gradient accumulation (8 micro-batches of 256 on one GPU) also keeps BN at 256 per forward pass, which is why it is the closest single-GPU stand-in; it costs wall-clock time, not accuracy.
issues.problem: Does not answer 'when is gradient accumulation the better option', and 'costs ... not accuracy' ignores that BN equivalence only holds if the micro-batch stays at 256.
issues.replacement: Gradient accumulation (8 micro-batches of 256 on one GPU) also keeps BN at 256 per forward pass, which is why it is the closest single-GPU stand-in; it costs wall-clock time, not accuracy, provided the micro-batch stays near 256. It is the better option when you do not have 8 GPUs or cannot fit a large per-GPU batch (for example 2 GPUs x 4 accumulation steps x 256 gives the same global 2048), when the all-reduce is the bottleneck (accumulate locally and synchronise once per optimiser step), or when you want a single-device reference run to debug the 8-GPU one. If memory forces micro-batches much smaller than 256, BN statistics become noisier than in the original run, so use SyncBN or GroupNorm or accept the difference.

issues.problem: Needs an explicit statement that this bug does not account for the reported ln 10 loss (verified: wrong-axis loss is ln B for random logits).
